Typological comparisons:
* First element (εὖ (eû)): сompare Latin bellus < duonus.
* Second element (μορφή (morphḗ)): сompare Latin fōrmōsus, fōrmō (< fōrma).
See bellus, fōrmōsus for more.

etymology_text: From βρόμα (vróma, “stench; dirty act”) + -ικος (-ikos), the former from an unattested Byzantine Greek *βρόμα (*bróma), nominal formation from Ancient Greek βρομέω (broméō) / βρομῶ (bromô, “to make loud noise”), from βρόμος (brómos, “loud noise”), from βρέμω (brémō, “to crash, to bang”). See also Ancient Greek βρῶμος (brômos, “stink, stench”), with which there is folk-etymological conflation (perhaps driven via semantic development "emanating noise" > "emanating (foul) smell"), as well as βρόμος (brómos, “oats”) and βρῶμᾰ (brômă, “shipworm”), which have also been conflated.

Also see the modern spelling καινούριος (kainoúrios).

etymology_text: From Byzantine Greek κουτσός (koutsós), of uncertain etymology. Likely from Middle Bulgarian коуцъ (kucŭ, “lame, crippled”), from Proto-Slavic *kucъ (“crippled, tailless”), of expressive origin. Another possibility is derivation from late Koine Greek κοξός (koxós, “lame”), borrowed from Late Latin coxus (“lame, crippled”), from Latin coxa (“hip, thigh”), from Proto-Indo-European *koḱs-.

examples.translation: The fisherman caught a huge fish.
examples.english: The fisherman caught a huge fish.

etymology_text: From Ancient Greek νωθρός (nōthrós), from νωθής (nōthḗs, “sluggish, lazy”).

examples.text:
Απάνω στο γιατάκι σου φίδι νωθρό κοιμάται,
Και φέρνει βόλτες ψάχνοντας τα ρούχα σου η μαϊμού.
examples.ref: 1979, “Θεσσαλονίκη [Thessaloniki]”, in Nikos Kavvadias (lyrics), Thanos Mikroutsikos (music), Ο Σταυρός του Νότου [Southern Cross], performed by Giannis Koutras:
examples.english:
On your bunk bed, a sluggish snake is sleeping,
And the monkey goes about, searching through your clothes.
examples.roman:
Apáno sto giatáki sou fídi nothró koimátai,
Kai férnei vóltes psáchnontas ta roúcha sou i maïmoú.
examples.translation:

And the monkey goes about, searching through your clothes.

glosses: sluggish, languid, lazy (having little motion, disinclined to move)

Inherited from Byzantine Greek σκάρτος (skártos), from Italian scarto + ending -ς (-s).

A rare Katharevousa compound, constructed as an alternative for the Hellenistic grammar term αὐτοπαθής (autopathḗs, “reflexive”).
Compound from the ancient ταὐτός (tautós, “the same”) ταὐτο- + Hellenistic Koine μεταβατός (metabatós), from μεταβαίνω (metabaínō, “pass over from one place to another”). From μετα- (meta-, “meta-”) μετά (metá) + βατός (batós, “passable”) < βαίνω (baínō).

etymology_text: From Ancient Greek ἀτελείωτος (ateleíōtos), morphologically α- (a-, “un-, a-, not”) + τελειώνω (teleióno, “to finish”).

examples.text: Με αυτό τον άνθρωπο έχω ατελείωτες ιστορίες!
examples.roman: Me aftó ton ánthropo écho ateleíotes istoríes!
examples.translation: I have endless dealings with this man!
examples.english: I have endless dealings with this man!

examples.text: Η πρώτη μέρα στην δουλειά μου φάνηκε ατελείωτη.
examples.roman: I próti méra stin douleiá mou fánike ateleíoti.
examples.translation: The first day at work seemed endless to me.
examples.english: The first day at work seemed endless to me.

examples.text:
Τα καλοκαίρια μας μικρά,
κι ατέλειωτοι οι χειμώνες.
examples.ref: 1980, “Μην Κλαις [Don't Cry]”, in Michalis Bourboulis (lyrics), Ilias Andriopoulos (music), Λαϊκά Προάστια [Popular Suburbs], performed by Sotiria Bellou:
examples.english:
Our summers short,
and our winters endless.
examples.roman:
Ta kalokaíria mas mikrá,
ki atéleiotoi oi cheimónes.
examples.translation:
Our summers short,
and our winters endless.

glosses: endless, unending, never-ending (never ending or seeming to end)

etymology_text: From Ancient Greek ἄπονος (áponos), morphologically ά- (á-, “un-, a-, not”) + πόνος (pónos, “pain”).

examples.text: Ήταν εντελώς άπονη προς τους άλλους.
examples.roman: Ítan entelós áponi pros tous állous.
examples.translation: She was completely uncaring towards others.
examples.english: She was completely uncaring towards others.

examples.text:
Άπονη ζωή, μας πέταξες στου δρόμου την άκρη,
μας αδίκησες.
examples.ref: 1965, “Άπονη ζωή [Heartless Life]”, Lefteris Papadopoulos (lyrics), Stavros Xarchakos (music), performed by Grigoris Bithikotsis:
examples.english:
Heartless life, you threw us to the side of the road,
You did us wrong.
examples.roman:
Áponi zoḯ, mas pétaxes stou drómou tin ákri,
mas adíkises.
examples.translation:
Heartless life, you threw us to the side of the road,
You did us wrong.

glosses: heartless, uncaring, unfeeling, unsympathetic (not caring about the pain or suffering of others)

etymology_text: Learned borrowing from Koine Greek σῠγκλητῐκός (sŭnklētĭkós), a calque from the Latin senātōrius. From σῠ́γκλητος (sŭ́nklētos, “senate”) + -κός (-kós), equivalent to συγ- (syg-, “with, together”) + κλητός (klitós, “called”) from verbal root κλη- of συγκαλώ (sygkaló), συν- (syn-) + καλώ (kaló, “to call, summon”), from Ancient Greek σῠγκᾰλέω (sŭnkăléō, “to call to council, convoke, convene”).

examples.roman: I mána tis tin eíche pánta mi vréxei kai mi stáxei kai epoménos den ítan étoimi na antimetopísei ton kósmo.
examples.translation: Her mother had always pampered and spoiled her so therefore she wasn't ready to face the world.
examples.english: Her mother had always pampered and spoiled her so therefore she wasn't ready to face the world.

examples.text:
Νιάου, σε έχουνε μη στάξει
κι είναι από μετάξι
η γούνα σου η γκρι.

examples.english:
Meow, they've got you pampered
And is made of silk
Your grey coat.
examples.roman:
Niáou, se échoune mi stáxei
ki eínai apó metáxi
i goúna sou i gkri.
examples.translation:
Meow, they've got you pampered
And is made of silk
Your grey coat.

examples.text:
Κι οι δάσκαλοι μου με είχανε
μη βρέξει και μη στάξει.
examples.ref: 1963, “Ο Μαθητής [The Student]”, in Charalampos Vasileiadis (lyrics), Giorgos Zampetas (music), Τα Κόκκινα Φανάρια [The Red Lanterns], performed by Giorgos Zampetas:
examples.english:
And my teachers
had me spoiled.
examples.roman:
Ki oi dáskaloi mou me eíchane
mi vréxei kai mi stáxei.

And my teachers
had me spoiled.

etymology_text:
From Byzantine Greek σπανός (spanós), from the first component of Koine Greek σπανοπώγων (spanopṓgōn, “who has a sparse beard”) (see πώγων (pṓgōn, “beard”) for the second component), further from σπάνιος (spánios, “rare, scarce”). Alternatively, directly from σπάνιος (spánios), with the same formation pattern seen in ὀρθός (orthós, “straight”) < ὄρθιος (órthios, “id”).
Despite similar phonetics and semantics, not related to σπαρνός (sparnós, “sparse, rare”) or Latvian spārns (“wing”). However, compare Romanian spân (“hairless”), Aromanian spãn, Sicilian spanu, which may derive from the same Ancient Greek root, possibly via a Vulgar Latin intermediate.
